en.content: The volume of oxygen required for complete combustion of 0.25 mole of methane at STP is
en.explanation:
Given,

Volume of methane $$=0.25 \mathrm{~mol}=5.6 \mathrm{~L}$$

[Multiply mole value by molar volume constant, 22.4 L]

Combustion of methane $$(\mathrm{CH}_4)$$

$$\underset{\text { Methane }}{\mathrm{CH}_4}+2 \mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$$

As, we know that, volume of 1 mole of gas is 22.4 L . Amount of oxygen is required for the combustion of 22.4 L of methane $$=(2 \times 22.4) \mathrm{L}=44.8 \mathrm{~L}$$

$$\therefore$$ Amount of oxygen required for the combustion of 5.6 L of methane

$$\begin{aligned} =\frac{44.8}{22.4} & \times 5.6=11.2 \mathrm{~L}=11.2 \mathrm{~dm}^3 \\ & {\left[\because 1 \mathrm{~L}=1 \mathrm{~dm}^3\right] } \end{aligned}$$

Hence, $$11.2 \mathrm{~dm}^3$$ of oxygen required for the complete combustion of 0.25 mole of methane.

en.content: A solution of $$\mathrm{CuSO}_4$$ is electrolysed using a current of 1.5 amperes for 10 minutes. What mass of Cu is deposited at cathode? [Atomic mass of $$\mathrm{Cu}=63.7$$]
en.explanation:
The mass of copper (Cu) deposited at the cathode can be calculated using Faraday's laws of electrolysis. The formula to find the mass deposited is :

$$ m = \frac{Q \times M}{n \times F} $$

where :

$ m $ is the mass of the substance deposited (in grams),

$ Q $ is the total electric charge passed through the solution (in coulombs),

$ M $ is the molar mass of the substance (in grams per mole),

$ n $ is the number of moles of electrons required to deposit one mole of the substance,

$ F $ is Faraday's constant ($ 96500 \, \text{C/mol} $).

First, calculate the total electric charge ($ Q $) :

$$ Q = I \times t $$

where :

$ I $ is the current (1.5 amperes),

$ t $ is the time (10 minutes = 600 seconds).

$$ Q = 1.5 \, \text{A} \times 600 \, \text{s} = 900 \, \text{C} $$

For copper ($\mathrm{Cu}$), the number of moles of electrons ($ n $) required to deposit one mole is 2 (since the reaction is $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}$).

Now, substitute the known values into the formula :

$$ m = \frac{900 \, \text{C} \times 63.7 \, \text{g/mol}}{2 \times 96500 \, \text{C/mol}} $$

$$ m = \frac{57330}{193000} \, \text{g} $$

$$ m = 0.297 \, \text{g} $$

Therefore, the mass of copper deposited at the cathode is 0.297 g.

Option B : 0.297 g

en.content: Silver crystallises in fcc structure, if edge length of unit cell is 316.5 pm . What is the radius of silver atom?
en.explanation:
Silver crystallizes in a face-centered cubic (fcc) structure. In an fcc structure, the relationship between the edge length ($a$) and the atomic radius ($r$) is given by :

$$ a = 2\sqrt{2}r $$

Given the edge length :

$$ a = 316.5 \, \text{pm} $$

We can solve for $r$ :

$$ 316.5 = 2\sqrt{2}r $$

$$ r = \frac{316.5}{2\sqrt{2}} $$

$$ r = \frac{316.5}{2 \times 1.414} $$

$$ r = \frac{316.5}{2.828} $$

$$ r \approx 111.91 \, \text{pm} $$

Thus, the radius of a silver atom is approximately $111.91$ pm.

Option B : 111.91 pm

en.content: A sonometer wire under suitable tension having specific gravity $$\rho$$, vibrates with frequency $$n$$ in air. If the load is completely immersed in water the frequency of vibration of wire will become
en.explanation:
The fundamental frequency of sonometer wire,

$$n=\frac{1}{2 L} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$$

As, $$L$$ and $$\mu$$ are constant, so $$n$$ depends on $$T$$.

$$n \propto \sqrt{T}$$

$$\therefore \frac{n_2}{n_1}=\sqrt{\frac{T_2}{T_1}}=\sqrt{\frac{(\text { Weight })_s-(\text { Weight })_w}{(\text { Weight })_s}}$$

$$=\sqrt{\frac{V_{\rho_s} g-V_{\rho_w} g}{V_{\rho_s} g}}=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{\rho_s}{\rho_w}-1}{\frac{\rho_s}{\rho_w}}}=\sqrt{\frac{\rho-1}{\rho}}$$

$$\begin{aligned} &\text { ( } \because \text { specific gravity of sonometer wire, } \rho=\frac{\rho_s}{\rho_w} \text { ) }\\ &\therefore \quad n_2=n \sqrt{\frac{\rho-1}{\rho}} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A radioactive nucleus emits $$4 \alpha$$-particles and $$7 \beta$$-particles in succession. The ratio of number of neutrons of that of protons, is [$$A=$$ mass number, $$Z=$$ atomic number]
en.explanation:
Let us assume, a particle $$X$$ having atomic number $$Z$$ and mass number $$A$$.

When an $$\alpha$$-particle is emitted by a nucleus, then its atomic number decreases by 2 and mass number decreases by 4. So, for given case,

$$z ^{X^A} \xrightarrow{4 \alpha \text {-particle }} z-8 ^{Y^{A-16}}$$

When a $$\beta$$-particle is emitted by a nucleus its atomic number increases by one and mass number remains unchanged. So, for given case,

$$Z-8 ^{Y^{A-16}} \xrightarrow{7 \beta \text {-particle }} Z-1 ^{Z^{A-16}}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore \frac{\text { Number of neutrons }}{\text { Number of protons }} & =\frac{(A-16)-(Z-1)}{(Z-1)} \\ & =\frac{A-Z-15}{(Z-1)} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: If the angle of dip at places $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$30^{\circ}$$ and $$45^{\circ}$$ respectively, then the ratio of horizontal component of earth's magnetic field at $$A$$ to that at $$B$$ will be $$\left[\sin 45^{\circ}=\cos 45^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \sin \frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{1}{2}, \cos \frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right]$$
en.explanation:
The horizontal component of earth's magnetic field,

$$H=B \cos \delta$$

At place $$A$$,

$$\begin{aligned} H_A & =B \cos \delta_A \\ & =B \cos 30^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3} B}{2} \end{aligned}$$

At place $$B$$,

en.content: The ratio of energy required to raise a satellite of mass $$m$$ to a height $$h$$ above the earth's surface of that required to put it into the orbit at same height is [$$R=$$ radius of the earth]
en.explanation:
The energy required to raise a satellite of mass m to a height h,

$$E_1=\frac{m g h}{\left(1+\frac{h}{R}\right)} \quad \text{... (i)}$$

$$\begin{aligned} &\text { The energy required to put it into orbit, }\\ &E_2=\frac{1}{2} m v_0^2=\frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{G M}{r}\right) \end{aligned}$$

$$\left(\because \text { orbital velocity, } v_0=\frac{G M}{r}\right)$$

$$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{G M}{R+h}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \frac{m g R^2}{R\left(1+\frac{h}{R}\right)}\left(\because G M=g R^2\right) \\ & =\frac{m g R}{2\left(1+\frac{h}{R}\right)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} &\text { The ratio of } E_1: E_2 \text { becomes, }\\ &\frac{E_1}{E_2}=\frac{m g h}{\left(1+\frac{h}{R}\right)} \times \frac{2\left(1+\frac{h}{R}\right)}{m g R}=\frac{2 h}{R} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A circular coil of radius $$R$$ has a resistance of $$40 \Omega$$. Figure shows two points $$P$$ and $$Q$$ on the circumference separated by a distance $$\frac{\pi R}{2}$$ which are connected to a 16 V battery with internal resistance of $$0.5 \Omega$$. What is the value of current $$I$$ flowing through the circuit?
en.explanation:
First, calculate the total resistance between points $ P $ and $ Q $ :

$$ \begin{aligned} R_{PQ} & = \left( \frac{30 \Omega \times 10 \Omega}{30 \Omega + 10 \Omega} \right) + 0.5 \Omega \\\\ & = \frac{300 \Omega}{40 \Omega} + 0.5 \Omega \\\\ & = 7.5 \Omega + 0.5 \Omega \\\\ & = 8 \Omega \end{aligned} $$

Next, determine the current flowing through the circuit using Ohm's law : $ V = IR $

$$ I = \frac{V}{R_{PQ}} $$

Where $ V $ is the voltage of the source. Therefore,

$$ I = \frac{16 \text{ V}}{8 \Omega} = 2 \text{ A} $$

The current $ I $ flowing through the circuit is thus 2 A.

en.content: An $$\alpha$$-particle of energy 10 eV is moving in a circular path in uniform magnetic field. The energy of proton moving in the same path and same magnetic field will be [mass of $$\alpha$$-particle $$=4$$ times mass of proton]
en.explanation:
The radius of circular path of charged particlein uniform magnetic field,

$$R=\frac{m v}{q B}\quad \text{.... (i)}$$

The kinetic energy of charged particle,

$$\begin{aligned} & K=\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \\ \Rightarrow \quad & v=\sqrt{\frac{2 K}{m}} \quad \text{.... (ii)} \end{aligned}$$

Substituting Eq. (ii) in Eq. (i), we get

$$R=\frac{m \sqrt{\frac{2 K}{m}}}{q B}=\frac{\sqrt{2 m K}}{q B}$$

For proton,

$$R_p=\frac{\sqrt{2 m_p K_p}}{q_p B} \quad \text{.... (iii)}$$

where, mass of proton is $$m_p$$, kinetic energy of proton is $$K_p$$ and charge on proton is $$q_p$$.

Similarly, for $$\alpha$$-particle,

$$R_\alpha=\frac{\sqrt{2 m_\alpha K_\alpha}}{q_\alpha B}\quad \text{.... (iv)}$$

where, mass of $$\alpha$$-particle is $$m_\alpha$$, charge on $$\alpha$$-particle is $$q_\alpha$$ and kinetic energy of $$\alpha$$-particle is $$K_\alpha$$.

Here, $$m_a=4 m_p$$ and $$q_a=2 q_p$$ Substituting value in Eq. (iv), we get

$$R_a=\frac{\sqrt{2\left\langle 4 m_p\right) K_a}}{B\left(2 q_p\right)}=\frac{\sqrt{2 m_p K_a}}{B q_p}$$

$$\begin{array}{rlrl} \therefore \quad \frac{R_p}{R_\alpha} =\sqrt{\frac{K_p}{K_\alpha}} \\ \quad \text { As, } R_p =R_\alpha \quad \text{(given)}\\ \therefore \quad K_\alpha \quad =K_p=10 \mathrm{eV} \end{array}$$

en.content: A thin light weight rod of diamagnetic substance such as silver is suspended in uniform external magnetic field. It will align itself with its length

options.content: inclined at an angle $$45^{\circ}$$ to magnetic field
inclined at an angle $$120^{\circ}$$ to magnetic field

en.explanation:
When a thin, lightweight rod made of a diamagnetic material such as silver is suspended in a uniform external magnetic field, it will align itself with its length perpendicular to the magnetic field.

Diamagnetic substances are materials that become weakly magnetized in the direction opposite to the applied external magnetic field. As a result, in a uniform magnetic field, a freely suspended diamagnetic rod will position itself perpendicular to the magnetic field.

en.content: A batsman hits a ball of mass 0.2 kg straight towards the bowler without changing its initial speed of $$6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$$. What is the impulse imparted to the ball?
en.explanation:
The impulse is equals to change in linear momentum.

$$\begin{aligned} \text { Change in momentum } & =m(v-u) \\ & =0.2(-6-6)=-2.4 \end{aligned}$$

The negative sign shows the direction of impulse is from batsman to bowler.

en.content: There are four convex lenses $$L_1, L_2, L_3$$ and $$L_4$$ of focal length $$2,4,6$$ and 8 cm, respectively. Two of these lenses from a telescope of length 10 cm and magnifying power 4. The objective and eye lenses are respectively
en.explanation:
Let us assume, the focal length of eyepiece and objective lens of telescope be $$f_e$$ and $$f_0$$, respectively.

The magnifying power of telescope,

$$\begin{array}{ll} & M=\frac{f_o}{f_e}=4 \\ \therefore \quad & f_o=4 f_e\quad \text{.... (i)} \end{array}$$

$$ \begin{aligned} &\text { The length of telescope is given by }\\ &\begin{aligned} L & =f_o+f_e \\ 10 & =f_o+f_e \\ 10 & =4 f_e+f_e \quad\left[\because f_o=4 f_e \text { from Eq. (i) }\right] \\ 5 f_e & =10 \\ f_e & =2 \mathrm{~cm} \\ \text { and } \quad f_o & =4 \times 2 \mathrm{~cm}=8 \mathrm{~cm} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$$

Hence, $$L_4$$ is the objective lens and $$L_4$$ is the eye lens.

en.content: The ratio of radii of gyration of a ring to a disc (both circular) of same radii and mass, about a tangential axis perpendicular to the plane is
en.explanation:
$$\begin{aligned} &\text { The radius of gyration is given by }\\ &K=\sqrt{\frac{I}{M}} \Rightarrow K \propto \sqrt{1} \end{aligned}$$

Moment of inertia of ring about tangential axis is calculated by parallel axis theorem, $$I_{\text {ring }}=I_c+M R^2 =M R^2+M R^2=2 M R^2$$

Similarly,

$$\begin{aligned} & I_{\text {disc }}=I_c+M R^2=\frac{1}{2} M R^2+M R^2=\frac{3}{2} M R^2 \\ & \therefore \quad \frac{K_{\text {ring }}}{K_{\text {disc }}}=\sqrt{\frac{I_{\text {ring }}}{I_{\text {disc }}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 M R^2}{\frac{3}{2} M R^2}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: An open organ pipe and a closed organ pipe have the frequency of their first overtone identical. The ratio of length of open pipe to that of closed pipe is
en.explanation:
The frequency higher than the fundamental frequency of sound is known as overtone.

For open organ pipe, first overtone is

$$\left(v_o\right)=\frac{2 v}{2 L_o}=\frac{v}{L_o}$$

For closed organ pipe, first overtone is

$$v_c=\frac{3 v}{4 L_c}$$

It is given that, their first overtone are identical

$$\begin{aligned} \text{i.e.,} \quad & v_o=v_c \\ & \frac{v}{L_o}=\frac{3 v}{4 L_c} \\ & \frac{L_o}{L_c}=\frac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A particle starting from rest moves along the circumference of a circle of radius $$r$$ with angular acceleration $$\alpha$$. The magnitude of the average velocity, in the time it completes the small angular displacement $$\theta$$ is
en.explanation:
The angular displacement of particle,

$$\theta=\omega_0 t+\frac{1}{2} \alpha t^2$$

$$\theta=\frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2 \quad \binom{\because \text { particle initially at rest }}{\therefore \omega_0=0}$$

$$t=\left(\frac{2 \theta}{\alpha}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$$

$$\begin{aligned} &\text { The average velocity of particle, }\\ &\begin{aligned} v_{\mathrm{avg}} & =\frac{\text { displacement }}{\text { time }} \\ & =\frac{r \theta}{t}=\frac{r \theta}{\left(\frac{2 \theta}{\alpha}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}=r\left(\frac{\theta \alpha}{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: Two spherical black bodies of radius $$r_1$$ and $$r_2$$ with surface temperature $$T_1$$ and $$T_2$$ respectively, radiate same power, then $$r_1: r_2$$ is
en.explanation:
The power radiated by the black body,

$$E=\varepsilon \sigma A T^4$$

It is given that, both spherical bodies radiate same power.

$$\therefore \quad E_1=E_2$$

$$\begin{aligned} &T_1^4 r_1^2=T_2^4 r_2^2 \text { (for spherical body, } A=4 \pi r^2 \text { ) }\\ &\Rightarrow \quad \frac{r_1}{r_2}=\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$

en.content: Which of the following instruments is not a direct reading instrument?
en.explanation: The potentiometer is used for measuring voltage or potential difference by comparison of an unknown voltage with the known voltage, hence it is not a direct reading instrument.

en.content: A block of mass $$m$$ is moving on rough horizontal surface with momentum $$p$$. The coefficient of friction between the block and surface is $$\mu$$. The distance covered by block before it stops is [$$g=$$ acceleration due to gravity]
en.explanation:
Using kinematic relation,

$$v^2=u^2-2 a s \quad \text{.... (i)}$$

The momentum $$p$$ is given by

$$\begin{aligned} p & =M u \\ u & =\frac{p}{M} \end{aligned}$$

and acceleration is given as $$a=\mu g$$

Substituting values in Eq. (i), we get

$$0=u^2-2 \text { as } \quad(\because \text { final velocity }, v=0)$$

$$0=\left(\frac{p}{M}\right)^2-2 \mu g s$$

$$\left(\frac{p}{M}\right)^2=2 \mu g s$$

$$\Rightarrow \quad s=\frac{p^2}{2 M^2 \mu g}$$

en.content: A large open tank containing water has two holes to its wall. A square hole of side $a$ is made at a depth $$y$$ and a circular hole of radius $$r$$ is made at a depth $$16 y$$ from the surface of water. If equal amount of water comes out through both the holes per second, then the relation between $$r$$ and $$a$$ will be
en.explanation:
$$\begin{aligned} &\text { Using principle of continuity, }\\ &A_1 v_1=A_2 v_2 \quad \text{... (i)} \end{aligned}$$

where, $$A_1$$ is the area of square hole, $$A_1=a^2$$,

$$A_2$$ is the area of circular hole, $$A_2=\pi r^2$$,

$$v_1$$ is the velocity at depth $$y, v_1=\sqrt{2 g y}$$

and $$v_2$$ is the velocity at depth $$16 \mathrm{y}, v_2=\sqrt{2 g(16 y)}$$.

Substituting values in Eq. (i), we get

$$\begin{aligned} a^2(\sqrt{2 g y}) & =\pi r^2(\sqrt{2 g(16 y)}) \\ a^2(\sqrt{2 g y}) & =4 \pi r^2(\sqrt{2 g y}) \\ r^2 & =\frac{a^2}{4 \pi} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore \quad r=\frac{a}{2 \sqrt{\pi}}$$

en.content: Refractive index of the medium is $$\mu$$ and wavelength is $$\lambda$$, then which of the following proportionality relation is correct?
en.explanation:
The refractive index of a medium is represented by $$\mu$$ and the wavelength is denoted by $$\lambda$$. Let's examine the proportionality relationship between these two variables.

Given:

$$\mu = \frac{c}{v} = \frac{\text{speed of light in vacuum}}{\text{speed of light in the medium}}$$

We can also express the speed of light in the medium as $v = \lambda f$, where $f$ is the frequency of the light wave. Since the frequency of light remains constant when transitioning between different media, we can rearrange the equation:

$$\mu = \frac{c}{v} = \frac{c}{\lambda f}$$

As $c$ and $f$ are constants, the refractive index $\mu$ is inversely proportional to the wavelength $\lambda$:

$$\mu \propto \frac{1}{\lambda}$$

en.content: $$A$$ transistor has a voltage gain $$A$$. If the amount $$\beta A$$ of its output is applied to the input of the transistor, then the transistor becomes oscillator, when
en.explanation:
The voltage gain of oscillator circuit is given by

$$A_f=\frac{A}{1-A \beta}$$

where, $$A$$ is the voltage gain without feedback and $$\beta$$ is called feedback factor.

For sustained oscillation, from Barkhausen criterion

$$A \beta=1$$

en.content: A spherical rubber balloon carries a charge, uniformly distributed over the surface. As the balloon is blown up and increases in size, the total electric flux coming out of the surface
en.explanation:
The electric field intensity due to point charged placed at the centre of a sphere of radius $$r$$,

$$E=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2}$$

As balloon is blown up, charge enclosed by the Gaussian surface remains same. So, electric field intensity remains same. The electric flux is given by

$$\begin{array}{rlrl} & \phi & =E \cdot d S \\ &\Rightarrow & \phi \propto E \end{array}$$

As, E remains same, the flux remains unchanged.

en.content: A diatomic gas undergoes adiabatic change. Its pressure $$p$$ and temperature $$T$$ are related as $$p \propto T^x$$, where $$x$$ is
en.explanation:
For a diatomic gas undergoing an adiabatic change, the relationship between pressure ($$p$$) and temperature ($$T$$) is given by:

$$\frac{T^\gamma}{p^{\gamma-1}} = \text{constant}$$

This can be rearranged to:

$$T^\gamma = \text{constant} \times p^{\gamma - 1}$$

Simplifying further, we get:

$$p \propto T^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}}$$

Given the problem states $$p \propto T^x$$, we compare the exponents to find:

$$x = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}$$

For a diatomic gas, the adiabatic index $$\gamma$$ is $$\frac{7}{5}$$. Therefore, we calculate:

$$x = \frac{\frac{7}{5}}{\frac{7}{5} - 1}$$

Simplifying the expression:

$$x = \frac{\frac{7}{5}}{\frac{2}{5}} = \frac{7}{2} = 3.5$$

Thus, for a diatomic gas undergoing an adiabatic process, the value of $$x$$ is 3.5.

en.content: The ratio of energies of photons produced due to transition of electron of hydrogen atom from its (i) second to first energy level and (ii) highest energy level to second level is respectively
en.explanation:
The energy of photons is given by

$$E=R h c\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2}-\frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$$

where, $$R$$ is Rydberg constant, $$h$$ is Planck's constant and $$c$$ is the speed of light.

(i) Energy of photon produced from second to first energy level,

$$\begin{aligned} & E_1=R h c\left(\frac{1}{1^2}-\frac{1}{2^2}\right) \\ & E_1=\frac{3}{4} R h c \end{aligned}$$

(ii) Energy of photon produced from highest energy level (i.e., $$\infty$$) to second level,

$$\begin{aligned} & E_2=R h c\left(\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{\infty}\right)=\frac{1}{4} R h c \\ \therefore \quad & \frac{E_1}{E_2}=\frac{\frac{3}{4} R h c}{\frac{1}{4} R h c}=\frac{3}{1} \text { or } 3: 1 \end{aligned}$$

en.content: As we go from the equator of the earth to pole of the earth, the value of acceleration due to gravity

options.content: decreases up to latitude of $$45^{\circ}$$ and increases thereafter

en.explanation: The acceleration due to gravity increases as we go from equator of earth to pole of earth because the equatorial radius is more than the polar radius of earth and $$g \propto \frac{1}{R}$$.

en.content: Two wires $$A$$ and $$B$$ are stretched by the same load. The radius of wire $$A$$ is double the radius of wire $$B$$. The stress on the wire $$B$$ as compared to the stress on the wire $$A$$ is
en.explanation:
Stress $$=\frac{\text { Force }}{\text { Area }}$$

The stress on wire $$A$$,

$$(\text {Stress})_A=\frac{F}{\pi r_A^2}=\frac{F}{\pi\left(2 r_B\right)^2} \text { (given, } r_A=2 r_B \text {)}$$

$$\begin{aligned} &\text { The stress on wire } B \text {, }\\ &\begin{array}{ll} & (\text { Stress })_B=\frac{F}{\pi r_B^2} \\ \therefore \quad & \frac{(\text { Stress })_B}{(\text { Stress })_A}=\frac{\frac{F}{\pi r_B^2}}{\frac{F}{\pi\left(2 r_B\right)^2}}=4 \\ \Rightarrow \quad & (\text { Stress })_B=4(\text {Stress})_A \end{array} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: When tension $$T$$ is applied to a sonometer wire of length $$I$$, it vibrates with the fundamental frequency $$n$$. Keeping the experimental setup same, when the tension is increased by 8 N, the fundamental frequency becomes three times the earlier fundamental frequency $$n$$. The initial tension applied to the wire (in newton) was
en.explanation:
The initial fundamental frequency of wire,

$$n=\frac{1}{2 L} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}\quad \text{.... (i)}$$

$$\begin{aligned} &\text { The final fundamental frequency of wire, }\\ &3 n=\frac{1}{2 L} \sqrt{\frac{T+8}{\mu}} \quad \text{... (ii)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} &\text { On dividing Eq. (ii) by Eq. (i), we get }\\ &\begin{aligned} \frac{3 n}{n} & =\frac{\frac{1}{2 L} \sqrt{\frac{T+8}{\mu}}}{\frac{1}{2 L} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}} \\ 3 & =\sqrt{\frac{T+8}{T}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 9 T & =T+8 \\ T & =1 \mathrm{~N} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: At absolute zero temperature, pure silicon behaves as
en.explanation:

At absolute zero temperature, its resistance becomes infinite and acts like an insulator.

en.content: Five capacitors each of capacity $$C$$ are connected as shown in figure. If their resultant capacity is $$2 \mu \mathrm{F}$$, then the capacity of each condenser is
en.explanation:
Given, resultant capacity, $$C_{\text {eq }}=2 \mu \mathrm{F}$$

The equivalent capacity of the circuit is given by

$$\frac{1}{C_{\text {eq }}}=\frac{1}{C}+\frac{1}{C}+\frac{1}{C}+\frac{1}{C}+\frac{1}{C}$$

($$\because$$ all capacitors are in series)

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{C_{\mathrm{eq}}} & =\frac{5}{C} \\ \frac{1}{2 \mu \mathrm{F}} & =\frac{5}{C} \\ \Rightarrow \quad C & =10 \mu \mathrm{F} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: The work done in blowing a soap bubble of radius $$R$$ is $$W$$. The work done in blowing a bubble of radius $$2 R$$ of the same soap solution is
en.explanation:
The work done in blowing a soap bubble,

$$W=T \times A$$

where, $$T$$ is the surface tension and $$A$$ is the area of soap bubble.

$$\begin{aligned} & W=T \times 4 \pi R^2 \\ & W \propto R^2 \end{aligned}$$

So, $$\frac{W_1}{W_2}=\frac{R_1^2}{R_2^2}$$

$$\Rightarrow \quad W_2=W_1\left(\frac{2 R}{R}\right)^2=4 W$$

en.content: The $$x, y$$ components of vector $$\mathbf{P}$$ have magnitudes 1 and 3 and $$x, y$$ components of resultant of $$\mathbf{P}$$ and $$\mathbf{Q}$$ have magnitudes 5 and 6, respectively. What is the magnitude of $$\mathbf{Q}$$ ?
en.explanation:
Given :

$$\mathbf{P} = \hat{\mathbf{i}} + 3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}$$

Resultant :

$$\mathbf{R} = 5 \hat{\mathbf{i}} + 6 \hat{\mathbf{j}} = \mathbf{P} + \mathbf{Q}$$

Let's find the components of vector $$\mathbf{Q}$$ :

$ \Rightarrow \mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{R} - \mathbf{P} $

$ \mathbf{Q} = (5 \hat{\mathbf{i}} + 6 \hat{\mathbf{j}}) - (\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}) $

$ \mathbf{Q} = 4 \hat{\mathbf{i}} + 3 \hat{\mathbf{j}} $

To find the magnitude of $$\mathbf{Q}$$ :

$ |\mathbf{Q}| = \sqrt{(4)^2 + (3)^2} $

$ |\mathbf{Q}| = \sqrt{16 + 9} $

$ |\mathbf{Q}| = \sqrt{25} $

$ |\mathbf{Q}| = 5 \text{ units} $

en.content: The graph of kinetic energy against the frequency $$v$$ of incident light is as shown in the figure. The slope of the graph and intercept on $$X$$-axis respectively are
en.explanation:
For photoelectric effect,

$$(\mathrm{KE})_{\max }=h \nu-\phi_0$$

where, $$\phi_0$$ is the work function of metal.

On comparing the Eq. (i) with straight line equation $$y=m x+c$$, we get

Slope, $$m=h$$ and intercept on $$y, c=-\phi_0$$ and $$\phi_0=h v_0$$

where, $$v_0$$ is threshold frequency.

So, for the graph of kinetic energy (KE) against the frequency ($$v$$).

Slope $$=$$ Planck's constant

and intercept on $$X$$-axis = threshold frequency

en.content: The length of solenoid is $$I$$ whose windings are made of material of density $$D$$ and resistivity $$\rho$$. The winding resistance is $$R$$. The inductance of solenoid is [$$m=$$ mass of winding wire, $$\mu_0=$$ permeability of free space]
en.explanation:
$$\begin{aligned} &\text { The self-inductance of solenoid, }\\ &L=\mu_0 N^2 \frac{A}{l}\quad \text{.... (i)} \end{aligned}$$

where, $$A$$ is the area of cross-section of solenoid and $$N$$ is number of turns.

If $$x$$ is the length of wire, then

$$R=\frac{\rho x}{A} \text { and } m=A x D$$

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad R m & =\frac{\rho x}{A}(A x D) \\ \Rightarrow \quad x & =\sqrt{\frac{R m}{\rho D}}\quad \text{.... (ii)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\text { Also, } x=2 \pi r N \Rightarrow N=\frac{x}{2 \pi r}=\frac{1}{2 \pi r} \sqrt{\frac{R m}{\rho D}}\quad \text{[from Eq. (ii)]]}$$

$$\begin{aligned} &\text { Substituting values in Eq. (i), we get }\\ &\begin{aligned} L=\mu_0\left(\frac{\sqrt{R m}}{2 \pi r \sqrt{\rho D}}\right)^2 \times \frac{A}{l} & =\mu_0 \frac{R m}{4 \pi^2 r^2 \rho D} \cdot \frac{\pi r^2}{l} \\ & =\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi I}\left(\frac{R m}{\rho D}\right) \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A step-up transformer has 300 turns of primary winding and 450 turns of secondary winding. A primary is connected to 150 V and the current flowing through it is 9A. The current and voltage in the secondary are
en.explanation:
Given that, number of turns in primary winding, $$N_p=300$$

Number of turns in secondary winding, $$N_S=450$$

Primary voltage, $$V_P=150 \mathrm{~V}$$

Primary current, $$I_P=9 \mathrm{~A}$$

For step-up transformer,

$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{V_S}{V_P}=\frac{N_S}{N_P} \\ & \frac{V_S}{150}=\frac{450}{300} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad V_S=\frac{450}{300} \times 150 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad V_S=225 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned}$$

Again, $$V_P I_P=V_S I_S$$

$$\begin{aligned} 150 \times 9 & =225 \times I_S \\ I_S & =\frac{1350}{225}=6.0 \mathrm{~A} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A simple pendulum of length $$I$$ has a bob of mass $$m$$. It executes SHM of small amplitude A. The maximum tension in the string is ($$g=$$ acceleration due to gravity)
en.explanation:
Consider the figure shown below

The string possess maximum tension when bolls at mean position of oscillation i.e., at position $$R$$.

From geometry, $$O P=\sqrt{1^2-A^2}$$

Also, $$\quad R P=O R-O P=I-\sqrt{1^2-A^2}$$

The whole kinetic energy of bob at position $$R$$ is converted into its potential energy at position $$B$$.

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \frac{1}{2} m v^2 & =m g\left(I-\sqrt{I^2-A^2}\right) \\ v^2 & =2 g\left(I-\sqrt{I^2-A^2}\right) \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} &\text { Balancing forces at } R \text {, }\\ &\begin{aligned} T-m g & =\frac{m v^2}{I}=\frac{2 m g\left(I-\sqrt{l^2-A^2}\right)}{I} \\ \therefore \quad T & =m g+2 m g\left(1-\sqrt{1-\frac{A^2}{l^2}}\right) \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$$

$$\text { Using approximation, } \sqrt{1-x^2}=1-\frac{x^2}{2} \text { for } x<<1 \text {, we }$$

$$\begin{aligned} T & =m g+2 m g\left[1-\left(1-\frac{A^2}{2^2}\right)\right] \\ & =m g+m g\left(\frac{A}{I}\right)^2 \\ & =m g\left[1+\left(\frac{A}{I}\right)^2\right] \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A block of mass $$m$$ attached to one end of the vertical spring produces extension $$x$$. If the block is pulled and released, the periodic time of oscillation is
en.explanation:
For vertical spring, the periodic time of oscillation is

$$T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$$

As, restoring force, $$|F|=kx$$

$$\begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow & k=\frac{F}{x}=\frac{m g}{x} \\ \therefore & T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{\frac{m g}{x}}}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{x}{g}} \end{array}$$

en.content: The resultant of two vector $$\mathbf{A}$$ and $$\mathbf{B}$$ is $$\mathbf{C}$$. If the magnitude of $$\mathbf{B}$$ is doubled, the new resultant vector becomes perpendicular to A. Then, the magnitude of $$\mathbf{C}$$ is
en.explanation:
Given, $$\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{C}$$

Resultant of $$A$$ and $$B$$ is

$$|C|=\sqrt{|\mathbf{A}|^2+|\mathbf{B}|^2+2|\mathbf{A}||\mathbf{B}| \cos \theta} \quad \text{... (i)}$$

When magnitude of B is doubled, new resultant (R$$_1$$) is perpendicular to A.

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \left|\mathbf{R}_1\right| \cdot \mathbf{A} & =0 \\ |\mathbf{A}+2 \mathbf{B}| \cdot \mathbf{A} & =0 \\ |\mathbf{A}|^2+2|\mathbf{A}||\mathbf{B}| \cos \theta & =0 \\ \cos \theta & =\frac{-|\mathbf{A}|}{2|\mathbf{B}|} \end{aligned}$$

Substituting this value in Eq. (i), we get

$$\begin{array}{cc} & |C|=\sqrt{|\mathbf{A}|^2+|B|^2+2|\mathbf{A}||\mathbf{B}|\left(\frac{-|\mathbf{A}|}{2|B|}\right)} \\ \Rightarrow & |C|^2=|\mathbf{A}|^2-|\mathbf{A}|^2+|\mathbf{B}|^2 \\ & |\mathbf{C}|^2=|\mathbf{B}|^2 \\ \therefore & |C|=|B| \operatorname{or} C=B \end{array}$$

en.content: A ray of light travelling through glass of refractive index $$\sqrt{2}$$ is incident on glass-air boundary at an angle of incidence $$45^{\circ}$$. If refractive index of air is 1 , then the angle of refraction will be $$\left[\sin 45^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \sin 90^{\circ}=1\right]$$
en.explanation:
$$\begin{aligned} &\text { From Snell's law, }\\ &\mu_i \sin i=\mu_r \sin r \end{aligned}$$

where, refractive index of glass is $$\mu_i$$, angle of incidence is $$i$$, refractive index of air is $$\mu_r$$ and angle of refraction is $$r$$.

$$\begin{aligned} & \text { Here, } \mu_i=\sqrt{2}, i=45^{\circ} \text { and } \mu_r=1 \\ \Rightarrow\quad & \begin{aligned} (\sqrt{2}) \sin 45^{\circ} & =(1) \sin r \\ (\sqrt{2})\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) & =\sin r \\ \Rightarrow \quad \sin r=1 & =\sin 90^{\circ} \\ r & =90^{\circ} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A particle of mass $$m$$ is performing UCM along a circle of radius $$r$$. The relation between centripetal acceleration $$a$$ and kinetic energy $$E$$ is given by
en.explanation:
Let the velocity of the particle be $$v$$.

The kinetic energy possessed by the particle in uniform circular motion,

$$\begin{aligned} & E=\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \\ & v^2=\frac{2 E}{m} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} &\text { The acceleration of the particle in circular motion, }\\ &a=\frac{v^2}{r}=\frac{2 E / m}{r} \Rightarrow a=\frac{2 E}{m r} \end{aligned}$$

en.content:
In conversion of moving coil galvanometer into an ammeter of required range, the resistance of ammeter, so formed is

[$$S=$$ shunt and $$G=$$ resistance of galvanometer]
en.explanation:
A moving coil galvanometer can be converted into an ammeter by connecting a low resistance (called shunt resistance) in parallel to it.

Hence, the resistance $$(\boldsymbol{R})$$ of the ammeter, so formed is

$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{S}+\frac{1}{G} \\ & R=\frac{S G}{S+G} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A square frame of each side $$L$$ is dipped in a soap solution and taken out. The force acting on the film formed is ($$T=$$ surface tension of soap solution)
en.explanation:
The surface tension is given by

$$T=\frac{F}{L}$$

For soap film, force on single side of square frame,

$$F=2 T L \quad$$ (film has two surfaces)

Hence, force on four sides of square frame,

$$F=4(2 T L)=8 T L$$
